entries.title: Don’t say it’s green! How green framing can depress support for renewable energy
entries.abstract: Abstract The green transition implies a shift towards renewable energies. However, their deployment has faced some backlash. This article assesses whether (a) the type of renewables and (b) framing can affect support for deployment. Through a survey experiment, three types of renewables (hydropower, onshore wind, offshore wind) and three types of frames (energy sovereignty, economic competitiveness, green transition) are evaluated, in general and for two typically skeptical groups (the least climate-worried and the less-educated ruralites). Using the case of Norway, we find strong effects for the type of renewables but little evidence for general framing effects. There are two exceptions: green framing has a negative effect on support for renewables where citizens have more fluid preferences (offshore wind) and depresses support among the least climate-worried and the less-educated rural…

entries.title: Not yet partisan: Cultural Theory explains attitudes about solar radiation management in the US
entries.abstract: This article investigates the role of Cultural Theory (CT) in explaining attitudes towards solar radiation management (SRM) in the US. Partisanship traditionally provides a clear lens through which to view favourability to climate change policies; however, the lack of partisan attention to geoengineering policies, such as SRM, suggests other belief systems may be better explainers of attitudes. Previously, scholars have found climate attitudes to vary based upon cultural types, which are a function of how individuals see the role of authority in policy making and the extent to which individuals see themselves as part of a social unit. We find that partisanship is a weak predictor of SRM attitudes, while cultural affinities provide strong influences over SRM attitudes. entries.title: Every Mile Counts: Geographical Distance as Administrative Burden in Intellectual Property Services
entries.abstract: Abstract While existing research has examined procedural and informational sources of administrative burden, this paper examines how organizational design choices about the geographic location of administrative authority institutionalize spatial burdens on firms. We leverage China's decentralization reform in trademark registration services as a natural experiment to test this theory. This reform reduced geographic distance by establishing local acceptance windows across the country from 2016 to 2019. Prior to this reform, trademark applications had to be submitted exclusively at the centralized Beijing office, imposing substantial geographic barriers on firms nationwide. entries.title: How cultural world views moderate policy framing on Universal Basic Income
entries.abstract: Universal Basic Income (UBI) has gained global attention as a potential policy response to the AI revolution, yet public support remains divided. While existing research highlights the role of political predisposition in shaping attitudes towards UBI, such explanations rely on the presence of partisan/ideological cues. In contexts where UBI is not yet politicized, ideological alignment may offer limited explanatory power. This article examines how individuals’ cultural predispositions, as conceptualized by Cultural Theory (CT), shape responses to different UBI framings in Taiwan, a non-Western democracy where partisan cues on UBI are less salient. Using an online survey experiment, the article tests how cultural world views interact with framing conditions to influence support for UBI. entries.title: Sick of change? Sickness absence following ownership conversions in Norwegian kindergartens
entries.abstract: Abstract The expansion of mixed-provider welfare systems has intensified debates about the consequences of public, nonprofit, and for-profit provision. Existing research focuses primarily on efficiency, service quality, and citizens' outcomes, while less is known about ownership conversions’ consequences for employees. We depart from research suggesting that ownership conversions can disrupt employee-organization value congruence as well as change the incentive structures. Leveraging population-wide administrative data from Norwegian childcare services (2015-2019), we examine whether ownership conversions are associated with changes in employee sickness absence. entries.title: Every Mile Counts: Geographical Distance as Administrative Burden in Intellectual Property Services
entries.abstract: Abstract While existing research has examined procedural and informational sources of administrative burden, this paper examines how organizational design choices about the geographic location of administrative authority institutionalize spatial burdens on firms. We leverage China's decentralization reform in trademark registration services as a natural experiment to test this theory. This reform reduced geographic distance by establishing local acceptance windows across the country from 2016 to 2019. Prior to this reform, trademark applications had to be submitted exclusively at the centralized Beijing office, imposing substantial geographic barriers on firms nationwide. entries.title: Dueling Political Fictions and Public Administration and Democracy in an Era of Populism and Authoritarian Impulses
entries.abstract: ABSTRACT The political fictions used in political discourse, during the English Civil War period, remain relevant to contemporary public policy and administration. Mainstream public administration discourse has too often employed the fiction of a singular and unbounded popular sovereignty that emerged during this period, leaving public administration ill‐equipped to deal with the authoritarian impulses of contemporary populist governments. What is needed in public administration discourse, in dealing with these authoritarian impulses, is not an ethic of administrative neutrality, such as has traditionally dominated much of our field, but an ethic of constitutionalism that draws on the fiction of the individual that was also articulated during the English Civil War period by the English Levellers and subsequently by the founders of the American Constitution.

Existing research focuses primarily on efficiency, service quality, and citizens' outcomes, while less is known about ownership conversions’ consequences for employees. entries.title: Don’t say it’s green! How green framing can depress support for renewable energy
entries.abstract: Abstract The green transition implies a shift towards renewable energies. However, their deployment has faced some backlash. This article assesses whether (a) the type of renewables and (b) framing can affect support for deployment. Through a survey experiment, three types of renewables (hydropower, onshore wind, offshore wind) and three types of frames (energy sovereignty, economic competitiveness, green transition) are evaluated, in general and for two typically skeptical groups (the least climate-worried and the less-educated ruralites). Using the case of Norway, we find strong effects for the type of renewables but little evidence for general framing effects. entries.title: Transparency and toxics: policy tool interactions in environmental regulation
entries.abstract: Abstract Toxics information disclosure programs have been hailed by some as being among the most successful environmental programs in history. Yet critics have argued that these policies may invite abuse by reducing traditional regulatory monitoring and enforcement, leading to poorer policy outcomes. Leveraging variation in U.S. state toxics transparency programs, we assess these conflicting claims. We find that information disclosure policies are associated with differences in agency monitoring and enforcement actions as well as with emission levels, but that these relationships are conditioned by the severity of the pollution problem. Overall, our evidence suggests that public information policies and traditional forms of regulation are imperfect substitutes, and successfully reducing toxic emissions requires both policy tools working in concert.

entries.title: A memory policy review: exploring perspectives on memory policies
entries.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the field of memory policy research within the broader study of memory politics. It asks how memory policies are conceptualized in existing scholarship and whether they are approached from a policy studies perspective. Previous research has addressed diverse memory-related practices but has failed to provide a consistent and policy-oriented conceptualization of memory policies. To address this gap, we integrate a scoping review with a systematic literature review structured through the PRISMA approach. We analyze peer-reviewed articles to map trends, assess conceptual uses, and reconstruct the notion of memory policies by examining how scholars define and evaluate them across different empirical contexts. Our findings demonstrate the need for a clearer, policy-focused framework to better understand the dynamics and implications of memory policies.

entries.title: The Geography of Local Politics: How Jurisdiction Size Shapes Local Policy Agendas
entries.abstract: Abstract One of the enduring questions in political science is whether large communities behave differently from small ones. While prior research has examined the political, democratic, and economic implications of community size, a key dimension remains underexplored: how political agendas differ across jurisdictions of varying sizes. This study addresses this gap by examining how the size and geography of local jurisdictions shape the size, issue diversity, complexity, and issue content of local policy agendas. Drawing on a systematic collection and coding of thousands of local council meeting agendas from Danish and Norwegian municipalities, the analysis reveals significant differences in agenda characteristics between large and small communities. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how jurisdiction size shapes democratic processes and local governance.

entries.title: How cultural world views moderate policy framing on Universal Basic Income
entries.abstract: Universal Basic Income (UBI) has gained global attention as a potential policy response to the AI revolution, yet public support remains divided. While existing research highlights the role of political predisposition in shaping attitudes towards UBI, such explanations rely on the presence of partisan/ideological cues. In contexts where UBI is not yet politicized, ideological alignment may offer limited explanatory power. This article examines how individuals’ cultural predispositions, as conceptualized by Cultural Theory (CT), shape responses to different UBI framings in Taiwan, a non-Western democracy where partisan cues on UBI are less salient. Using an online survey experiment, the article tests how cultural world views interact with framing conditions to influence support for UBI. entries.title: Power, politics, and policy agency: towards a Functional Theory of Agency
entries.abstract: This article examines how political position shapes policy agency in local policy making. Specifically, it asks: what patterns of policy agency functions do municipal councillors ( regidores ) exhibit in the local policy process? Drawing on the Functional Theory of Agency framework and a sequential mixed-methods design combining a national survey of Mexican municipal councillors with follow-up semi-structured interviews, we analyse how councillors exercise four modes of policy agency: steering, innovation, intermediation, and intelligence. Our findings reveal systematic differences between majoritarian and opposition councillors. Majoritarian councillors dominate commissions, align with mayoral priorities, and primarily act as steerers and brokers of executive policy. entries.title: Explaining the policy advisory success of non-governmental organisations in unlikely settings: a complexity-oriented approach
entries.abstract: The aim of this study is to explore under what conditions policy actors are able to achieve advisory influence in a contested policy-making space. Specifically, it focuses on the factors leading to the success of a set of advisory actors typically assumed to be among the most disadvantaged – non-governmental organisations (NGOs). The article departs from dominant approaches to studying influence relying on theoretical exclusivity and argues for the need to adopt more flexible complexity-oriented analytical styles. To illustrate this, the study uses the extreme case of Bulgaria’s social service delivery reform. The analysis of the case provides strong support for the need to employ greater analytic eclecticism rather than rigid theoretical assumptions based on a single explanatory theory in making sense of advisory influence. entries.title: Extending the Advocacy Coalition Framework: measuring within-coalition belief variation in offshore wind policy conflicts
entries.abstract: This study advances the Advocacy Coalition Framework (ACF) literature by introducing new approaches to capture variation in actors’ belief expression and to analyse how such expressions are constrained by actors’ organisational affiliations. Moving beyond existing accounts of constrained belief expression, it reconceptualises constraint as measurable differences in the breadth and intensity of beliefs articulated by actors within a coalition. Drawing on debates over US offshore wind energy, the study examines how organisational affiliation shapes patterns of constrained belief expression in public discourse. entries.title: A systematic review of policy conflict and its (un)productive consequences
entries.abstract: Like most collective decision-making processes, the formulation, adaptation, and implementation of public policies are not immune to conflict. Recently, various authors have lamented the lack of explicit attention to conflict in the policy process and called for more research into how policy conflicts unfold and what consequences they produce. This article contributes to that scholarship in two ways: first, through a systematic discussion of empirical studies on the consequences of policy conflict since 2000; and second, by bringing into conversation insights that are currently dispersed across fragmented research traditions. The systematic literature review focuses on three aspects: how and where policy conflicts have been studied; whether and how they have been conceptualised; and what their consequences are. entries.title: Not yet partisan: Cultural Theory explains attitudes about solar radiation management in the US
entries.abstract: This article investigates the role of Cultural Theory (CT) in explaining attitudes towards solar radiation management (SRM) in the US. Partisanship traditionally provides a clear lens through which to view favourability to climate change policies; however, the lack of partisan attention to geoengineering policies, such as SRM, suggests other belief systems may be better explainers of attitudes. Previously, scholars have found climate attitudes to vary based upon cultural types, which are a function of how individuals see the role of authority in policy making and the extent to which individuals see themselves as part of a social unit.
